title: The Leadership Perception Gap
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article examines the systematic gap between how leaders believe they are performing and how their teams actually experience their leadership — a disconnect with real consequences for team climate, morale, and performance. The core mechanism is that leaders judge themselves by their intentions and internal reasoning, while team members evaluate them on visible actions in real time; since teams only observe a small slice of what leaders actually do, visible behavior gets generalized into an assumed overall pattern. Research cited in the piece suggests leaders are particularly prone to overestimating their effectiveness in three domains: communication clarity (leaders believe they communicate more clearly than they do), approachability (believing themselves open to feedback when team members experience them as closed), and delegation (believing they empower others when teams experience micromanagement). The article argues that good intentions are consistently mistaken for strong impact, that leaders deflect feedback they believe lacks context, and that external feedback is therefore essential precisely because leaders will not self-correct misperceptions they don't believe they have.
points: Leaders judge themselves by their intentions and internal reasoning; team members judge them by their visible actions — this structural asymmetry produces systematic perception gaps that leaders are largely unaware of.

When observation is limited, team members generalize from visible behavior to the whole pattern: if a leader fails to hold someone accountable in one meeting, teams presume the same is true away from the meeting.

Leaders systematically overestimate their communication clarity, their approachability, and their degree of delegation — three domains where the perception gap has particularly damaging consequences for trust, candor, and team autonomy.

Because leaders confuse good intentions with strong impact, team member feedback on perception gaps rarely changes their view — they give themselves credit for effort that others can't see and deflect criticism they believe lacks context.

External feedback is essential precisely because leaders will not self-correct misperceptions they don't believe they have; the gap only closes when leaders receive structured, credible information from outside their own self-assessment.
quotes: How well a leader believes they are performing is often at odds with how the team experiences their leadership. Leaders and team members typically look at the same actions from very different vantage points.

A leader has direct access to their own intentions, constraints, and reasoning. They know exactly what they are trying to accomplish, what trade-offs they have considered, and what information they have to work from. As a result, leaders judge themselves primarily on their goals and intentions, while team members evaluate them largely on their actions in real time.

Team members only get to see a small slice of what leaders actually do, and this can amplify the gap in perception. When observation is limited, team members presume a leader's visible behavior reflects the whole pattern.

Research suggests leaders are particularly prone to overestimate how effectively they communicate, how approachable they are, and how much they delegate and empower others. These misperceptions can significantly shape the team dynamic.

Leaders also commonly overestimate how approachable they are. Because their intention is to encourage dissent, stay open to feedback, and listen to team members' problems and issues, they conclude that others find them more approachable and desirous of candid feedback than they are.

Because leaders confuse good intentions with strong impact, team member feedback on these and other gaps rarely changes their view. Leaders typically give themselves credit for effort others can't see and deflect criticism they believe lacks context.
